1.word_for_word: rājñaḥ praśnam abhinandati — he commends the king's question; varīyān iti — with the word 'most excellent'; te tvayā — by you; puṃsām śrotavya-ādiṣu madhye — among the subjects to be heard by people and the like; yaḥ paraḥ śreṣṭha-gocaraḥ praśnaḥ — the question whose subject is highest and best; kṛtaḥ — has been asked; eṣa varīyān — this is most excellent; yataḥ loka-hitam etat — because this benefits the world; mokṣa-hetutvāt — because it is a cause of liberation; ātma-vidām muktānām ca sammataḥ — approved by knowers of the Self and by liberated persons.
1.translation: The king's question is commended by the word 'most excellent.' The question you have asked, whose subject is the highest among all matters people may hear about, is indeed most excellent. It is beneficial to the world because it is a cause of liberation, and it is approved by knowers of the Self and by liberated persons.

2.word_for_word: tatra tāvat — first, in this connection; svābhāvika-kriyāṇām anartha-hetutvam vadan — stating that ordinary instinctive activities are causes of misfortune; brūhi yad vā viparyayam iti asya uttaram āha — he answers the earlier request 'tell me also the contrary'; śrotavyādīni iti tribhiḥ — in three verses beginning 'things to be heard'; gṛheṣu saktānām — of those attached to household life; ata eva gṛha-medhinām — therefore called gṛhamedhins; tad-gata-pañca-sūnā-parāṇām — occupied with the five household slaughters inherent in it; medhatiḥ hiṃsā-arthaḥ — the root medh has the sense of injury/slaughter.
2.translation: First, stating that ordinary instinctive activities become causes of misfortune, he answers the earlier request, 'Tell me also the contrary,' in the three verses beginning 'things to be heard.' Those attached to household affairs are therefore called gṛhamedhins and are occupied with the five unavoidable forms of injury connected with household life. The verbal root *medh* carries the sense of violence or slaughter.

3.word_for_word: taiḥ ca — by those activities as well; vṛthā eva āyuḥ vyayaḥ bhavati — life is spent entirely in vain; naktam rātrau yat vayaḥ āyuḥ — the portion of life at night; tat nidrayā vyavāyena ratyā vā hriyate — is taken away by sleep or sexual enjoyment; divā ahni yat vayaḥ — the portion of life by day; tad artha-artham udyamena — is spent striving for wealth; siddhe arthe kuṭumba-poṣaṇena vā — or, when wealth has been gained, maintaining the family; ca-kārau anukta-samuccaya-arthau — the two occurrences of 'and' include other unmentioned activities.
3.translation: Life is thus spent entirely in vain. The portion of one's life that passes at night is taken away by sleep or sexual enjoyment; the portion that passes by day is spent striving to obtain wealth or, once wealth has been obtained, maintaining the family. The two occurrences of the word 'and' also include other activities not explicitly mentioned.

4.word_for_word: nanu — objection; naśvara-kuṭumba-ādi-artham katham āyuḥ-vyayam kuryāt — why would anyone spend life for a perishable family and the like?; tatra āha — the verse answers; deha-ādiṣu — in body and the rest; ātmanaḥ sainyeṣu parikareṣu — which function as the self's army and retinue; asatsu mithyā-bhūteṣu api — although impermanent and falsely taken as belonging to the self; pramattaḥ prasaktaḥ — heedless and deeply attached; teṣām pitṛ-ādi-dṛṣṭāntena nāśam paśyan api — although seeing their destruction in the example of father and others; na anusandhatte — he does not reflect upon it.
4.translation: One may ask why a person would spend his life for a family and other things that are known to be perishable. The answer is that he is heedlessly attached to the body and the rest, his supposed army and retinue, although they are impermanent and falsely taken as his own. Even while seeing their destruction in the deaths of his father and others, he does not connect that observation with his own condition.

5.word_for_word: evam viparyaya-praśna-uttaram uktvā — having thus answered the question about the contrary course; śrotavya-ādi-praśnasya uttaram āha — he answers the question about what is to be heard and so on; tasmāt iti — with 'therefore'; he bhārata — O descendant of Bharata; sarva-ātmā iti preṣṭhatvam āha — 'the Self of all' indicates His being most dear; bhagavān iti saundaryam — 'Bhagavān' indicates beauty; īśvara iti āvaśyakatvam — 'Lord' indicates indispensability; hariḥ iti bandha-hāritvam — 'Hari' indicates His removing bondage; abhayam — fearlessness; mokṣam — liberation; icchatā — by one who desires it.
5.translation: Having answered the question about the mistaken course of life, he now answers the question concerning what should be heard and the like: 'Therefore, O descendant of Bharata...' 'The Self of all' indicates that He is the most beloved; 'Bhagavān' indicates His beauty; 'Lord' indicates that He is indispensable; and 'Hari' indicates that He removes bondage. 'Fearlessness' means liberation, which is what the seeker desires.

6.word_for_word: ataḥ param anyat śreyaḥ na asti — there is no good higher than this; etāvān eva janmanaḥ lābhaḥ phalam — this alone is the gain or fruit of birth; tam āha — he identifies it; nārāyaṇa-smṛtiḥ — remembrance of Nārāyaṇa; sāṅkhya-ādibhiḥ sādhyaḥ — it is attained through Sāṅkhya and the other means; iti teṣām svātantryeṇa lābhatvam vārayati — thus he denies that those disciplines have independent fruit; sāṅkhyam — Sāṅkhya; ātma-anātma-vivekaḥ — discrimination of Self and non-Self; yogaḥ aṣṭāṅgaḥ — Yoga is the eight-limbed discipline; ante tu smṛtiḥ paraḥ lābhaḥ — at the end remembrance is the supreme gain; na tat-mahimā vaktum śakyaḥ — its greatness cannot be fully expressed.
6.translation: There is no higher good than this. This alone is the true gain and fruit of human birth: remembrance of Nārāyaṇa. By saying that it is accomplished through Sāṅkhya, Yoga and the other disciplines, the verse denies that those disciplines yield an independent ultimate gain. Sāṅkhya is discrimination between Self and non-Self; Yoga is the eight-limbed discipline. At life's end, remembrance of Nārāyaṇa is the supreme gain, and its greatness cannot be fully expressed.

7.word_for_word: tatra sad-ācāram pramāṇayati — he adduces the conduct of the good as evidence; prāyeṇa iti — with the word 'generally'; vidhi-ṣedhataḥ — from injunction and prohibition; vidhi-niṣedhābhyām nivṛttāḥ — withdrawn from ritual injunctions and prohibitions; nairguṇye brahmaṇi sthitāḥ api — even those established in attributeless Brahman; sma — a particle indicating what is well known.
7.translation: He adduces the established conduct of the good as evidence, using the word 'generally.' Even those who have withdrawn from ritual injunctions and prohibitions and are established in attributeless Brahman are known to delight in narrating the qualities of Hari. The particle *sma* marks this as a well-known fact.

8.word_for_word: kim idam apūrvam kathayasi — 'Are you telling something unprecedented?'; satyam apūrvam eva idam — yes, this is indeed extraordinary; idam bhagavat-proktam — this Purāṇa was spoken by Bhagavān; tat-nāma-eka-pradhānam — and has His name as its principal subject; purāṇam brahma-sammitam — a Purāṇa equal to Brahman/the Veda; sarva-veda-tulyam — equal to all the Vedas; yad vā — alternatively; brahma samyak mitam yena — that by which Brahman is rightly measured/known; kutaḥ tvayā prāptam — from where did you obtain it?; adhītavān — I studied it; dvaipāyanāt pituḥ — from my father Dvaipāyana; dvāpara-ādau — at the beginning of the period called Dvāpara; dvāparaḥ ādiḥ yasya kālasya — the time whose beginning is Dvāpara; dvāpara-ante iti arthaḥ — meaning at the end of Dvāpara; śantanu-sama-kāle vyāsa-avatāra-prasiddheḥ — because Vyāsa's appearance is known to have been in Śantanu's time.
8.translation: One may ask, 'Are you telling something unprecedented?' Yes, this is indeed extraordinary. This Purāṇa was spoken by Bhagavān and has Him and His name as its principal subject; it is *brahma-sammita*, equal to all the Vedas—or, alternatively, that by which Brahman is rightly known. How did Śuka obtain it? He studied it from his father Dvaipāyana. 'At the beginning of Dvāpara' is interpreted as the period whose beginning is Dvāpara, hence the end of Dvāpara, since Vyāsa's appearance is known to belong to the time of Śantanu.

9.word_for_word: siddhasya tava kutaḥ adhyayane pravṛttiḥ — if you were already perfected, why did you undertake study?; tatra āha — to this he says; pariṇiṣṭhitaḥ api iti — with 'although fully established'; gṛhīta-cetāḥ — one whose mind was seized; ākṛṣṭa-cittaḥ — whose consciousness was attracted.
9.translation: If Śuka was already perfected, why did he undertake study? The verse answers with 'although fully established.' His mind was seized—his consciousness was irresistibly attracted—by the Lord's qualities and pastimes.

10.word_for_word: tad aham — therefore I; te — to you; mahā-pauruṣika — O one devoted to the Great Person; vakṣyāmi — I shall relate it; yathā adhītam — exactly as I studied it; yathā mati — according to my understanding; bhagavān paramaḥ puruṣaḥ — Bhagavān, the Supreme Person; yasmin satyam paraṃ dhīmahi — upon whom the supreme truth is contemplated.
10.translation: Therefore I shall relate it to you, O one devoted to the Great Person, exactly as I studied it and according to my understanding, for your mind is fixed upon Bhagavān, the Supreme Person.

11.word_for_word: sādhakānām siddhānām ca — for practitioners and perfected persons; na ataḥ param anyat śreyaḥ asti — there is no higher good than this; icchatām kāminām — for those who desire particular ends; tat-tat-phala-sādhanam etat eva — this alone is the means to each respective fruit; nirvidyamānānām mumukṣūṇām — for the disenchanted who seek liberation; mokṣa-sādhanam etat eva — this alone is the means to liberation; yoginām jñāninām — for yogins and jñānins; phalam ca etat eva — this itself is also the fruit; nirṇītam — established decisively; na atra pramāṇam vaktavyam — no further proof need be stated here.
11.translation: For practitioners and for the perfected there is no higher good than this. For those who desire particular ends, the repeated glorification of Hari's name is the means to their respective fruits; for seekers of liberation it is the means to liberation; and for yogins and jñānins it is itself the fruit. This conclusion is established decisively; no further proof needs to be stated here.

12.word_for_word: alpam eva āyuḥ avaśiṣṭam — only a little life remains; kim aham sādhayeyam — what can I accomplish?; iti mā śuca — do not grieve in this way; kim iti tribhiḥ — he answers in three verses beginning 'what use'; parokṣaiḥ alakṣitaiḥ hāyanaiḥ varṣaiḥ — years that pass unseen and unnoticed; viditam — consciously known; vṛthā yāti iti jñātam — recognized as otherwise passing in vain; yataḥ yena jñānena — because by that awareness; ghaṭeta — one should apply oneself; yatnam kuryāt — one should make effort.
12.translation: Do not grieve, thinking, 'Only a little of my life remains; what can I accomplish?' The answer is given in the three verses beginning 'what use.' Many years may pass unseen and unnoticed; better is a single moment consciously recognized as otherwise liable to pass in vain, because with that awareness one can apply oneself and make the necessary effort for the highest good.

13.word_for_word: khaṭvāṅgaḥ hi deva-pakṣe sthitvā — Khaṭvāṅga, having fought on the side of the gods; daityān ajayat — conquered the demons; tataḥ prasannaiḥ devaiḥ varam vṛṇīṣva iti ukte — when the pleased gods told him 'choose a boon'; tena uktam — he replied; prathamam tāvat mama āyuḥ kathyatām — first tell me the length of my remaining life; tat tu muhūrta-mātram asti — it is only one muhūrta; tataḥ ati-śīghram vimānena bhuvam āgatya — then very quickly returning to earth by celestial vehicle; harim śaraṇam gataḥ — he took refuge in Hari; svarga-bhūmiḥ rajaḥ-adhikā — heaven is dominated by rajas; karma-bhūmiḥ pṛthvī — the earth is the field of action.
13.translation: Khaṭvāṅga fought on the side of the gods and conquered the demons. When the pleased gods told him to choose a boon, he first asked them to tell him how much life remained. They answered that only a single muhūrta remained. He therefore returned to earth with great speed in a celestial vehicle and took refuge in Hari. Heaven is a realm in which rajas predominates, whereas the earth is the field in which decisive spiritual action is performed.

14.word_for_word: tava tu etarhi api — for you, even now; idānīm api — even at this very time; tāvat iti — 'within that much time'; tāvatā kālena — within that period; sāmparāyikam — what concerns the next world; pāralaukikam sādhanam — the means directed toward the hereafter; sampādaya — accomplish it.
14.translation: For you too, even now, there is time. 'Within that much time' means: within the seven days remaining, accomplish the means that pertains to the next world.

15.word_for_word: tatra vairāgyam tāvat āha — first he teaches dispassion; anta-kāla iti — with the verse beginning 'when the final time has come'; gata-sādhvasaḥ — one from whom fear has gone; mṛtyu-bhaya-śūnyaḥ — free from fear of death; asaṅgaḥ nāma anāsaktiḥ — nonattachment means absence of clinging; tena śastreṇa — with that as a weapon; spṛhām sukha-icchām — longing, the desire for pleasure; tam deham anu ye putra-kalatra-ādayaḥ — those such as sons and wife who follow upon identification with the body; teṣu api spṛhām chindyāt — one should cut off longing for them as well.
15.translation: First he teaches dispassion. One whose final time has come should be free from fear of death. Nonattachment means absence of clinging, and with that as a weapon he should cut away the longing for bodily pleasure and also the longing directed toward those—such as sons and wife—whose relation depends upon the body.

16.word_for_word: gṛhāt pravrajitaḥ nirgataḥ — gone forth and departed from home; gṛhe sthitasya punaḥ api āsakti-sambhavāt — because attachment may arise again for one who remains there; tatra aṣṭāṅga-yogam āha — here he begins the eight-limbed yoga; dhīra iti brahmacarya-ādi-yama-upalakṣaṇam — 'steady' indicates restraints such as celibacy; puṇya-tīrtha iti snāna-ādi-niyama-upalakṣaṇam — 'sacred tīrtha' indicates observances such as bathing; āsanam āha śucau iti — the seat is indicated by 'in a pure place'; vivikte ekānte — secluded, solitary; vidhivat — according to rule; kuśa-ajina-cailaiḥ krameṇa nirmite — prepared in order with kuśa grass, deerskin and cloth.
16.translation: He should go forth and leave home, because attachment may arise again while one remains there. The verse then begins the eight-limbed yoga. 'Steady' indicates the restraints such as celibacy; bathing at a sacred tīrtha indicates the observances; and the seat is to be in a pure, solitary place, prepared according to rule with kuśa grass, deerskin and cloth in order.

17.word_for_word: japa-garbham prāṇāyāmam vaktum — in order to teach prāṇāyāma containing japa; japyam āha — he first states what is to be repeated; trivṛd-brahmākṣaram — the threefold syllable of Brahman; tribhiḥ akāra-ādibhiḥ vartitam grathitam — formed and woven from the three letters beginning with a; brahmākṣaram praṇavam — the Brahman-syllable, praṇava Oṁ; manasā abhyaset āvartayet — one should mentally practice and repeat it; prāṇāyāmena mano-niyamanam āha — he teaches restraint of the mind through breath regulation; mano yacchet vaśīkuryāt — one should bring the mind under control; brahma-bījam praṇavam avismaran — without forgetting praṇava, the seed of Brahman; jita-śvāsaḥ san — while having mastered the breath.
17.translation: To teach prāṇāyāma containing japa, he first states the syllable to be repeated. The threefold Brahman-syllable is praṇava, Oṁ, formed from the three letters beginning with *a*; one should repeat it mentally. Then he teaches control of the mind through regulation of the breath: having mastered the breath and without forgetting praṇava, the seed of Brahman, one should bring the mind under control.

18.word_for_word: pratyāhāram āha — he teaches withdrawal of the senses; niyacchet nigṛhṇīyāt — one should restrain them; akṣān indriyāṇi — 'akṣa' means the senses; niścaya-ātmikā buddhiḥ sārathiḥ yasya — one whose charioteer is discriminative intelligence; dhāraṇām āha — he teaches concentration; manaḥ iti — with 'the mind'; punaḥ ca karmabhiḥ tad-vāsanābhiḥ ākṣiptam ākṛṣṭam — the mind repeatedly drawn away by actions and their latent impressions; śubha-arthe bhagavad-rūpe — toward the auspicious object, the form of Bhagavān.
18.translation: He now teaches withdrawal of the senses: one should restrain the *akṣas*, the senses, with discriminative intelligence as charioteer. He then teaches concentration. The mind, repeatedly drawn away by actions and by the latent impressions those actions leave behind, is to be brought back to the auspicious object—the form of Bhagavān.

19.word_for_word: dhyānam āha — he teaches meditation; tatra iti — with 'there'; ekam — one; ekaṃ pāda-ādi avayavam — one limb at a time, beginning with the feet; avyucchinnena — without interruption; samagra-rūpāt aviyuktena — not separated from awareness of the complete form; āśraya-viśeṣeṇa sāmānyataḥ citta-sthirīkaraṇam dhāraṇā — dhāraṇā is stabilizing the mind generally upon a particular support; avayava-vibhāvanayā tad-dārḍhyam dhyānam — meditation is the strengthening of that stability through contemplation of the limbs; samādhim āha — he teaches samādhi; nirviṣayam manaḥ yuṅktvā samādhāya — settling the mind without external object; sthirībhūte manasi — when the mind has become steady; sphurat-paramānanda-mātra-ākāram kṛtvā — making it take the form of pure manifest supreme bliss; prasīdati upaśāmyati — it becomes serene and quiet.
19.translation: He next teaches meditation. 'One' means one limb at a time, beginning with the feet, without losing awareness of the complete form. Dhāraṇā is the general stabilization of the mind upon a particular support; dhyāna is the deepening of that stability by sustained contemplation of the individual limbs. He then indicates samādhi: when the mind is settled free from other objects and has become steady, it assumes the form of pure manifest supreme bliss and becomes serene and completely quiet.

20.word_for_word: guṇa-vaśāt punaḥ api kṣobhe sati — if agitation again arises under the influence of the guṇas; dhāraṇām eva sthirīkuryāt — one should re-establish concentration itself; rajasā ākṣiptam — pulled away by rajas; tamasā vimūḍham — stupefied by tamas; svīyam manaḥ nirundhyāt — one should restrain one's own mind; tat-kṛtam — produced by them; rajas-tamobhyām kṛtam — produced by rajas and tamas.
20.translation: If agitation again arises under the influence of the guṇas, one should re-establish concentration. One should restrain one's own mind when it is pulled away by rajas or stupefied by tamas. The impurity that concentration destroys is precisely that which is produced by rajas and tamas.

21.word_for_word: yataḥ — because; yasyām kriyamāṇāyām — when this concentration is being practiced; bhadram sukha-ātmakam āśrayam viṣayam paśyataḥ — for one who beholds the auspicious, blissful support as the object; tatra eva prītiḥ bhavati — love arises toward that very object.
21.translation: When this concentration is practiced and the meditator beholds the auspicious support whose nature is bliss, love arises toward that very object.

22.word_for_word: yathā yatra yādṛśī ca — how, where and of what kind; iti-kartavyatā-viṣaya — concerning the procedure to be performed; tat-tad-viśeṣāṇām praśnāḥ — questions about each of those particular details.
22.translation: The words 'how,' 'where,' and 'of what kind' ask respectively about the particular details of the procedure: how the concentration is to be performed, upon what it is to be fixed, and what its object is like.

23.word_for_word: yathā iti asya uttaram — the answer to the question 'how?'; jitāsana iti — is given by 'one who has mastered the posture'; viṣayam āha — he states the object; sthūla iti — with the word 'gross'; sārdhena — together with the following half-verse.
23.translation: The phrase beginning 'one who has mastered the posture' answers the question 'how?' The word 'gross,' together with the following half-verse, introduces the answer concerning the object upon which the mind is to be fixed.

24.word_for_word: viśeṣa iti — on the word 'particular manifestation'; viśeṣaḥ virāḍ-dehaḥ — the particular form is the body of Virāṭ; ati-sthūlānām api sthūlataraḥ — grosser even than extremely gross things; sat iti — the word 'existent'; kārya-mātram — means the entire realm of manifested effects.
24.translation: The 'particular manifestation' is the body of Virāṭ, grosser even than things that are already extremely gross. The word *sat*, 'existent,' denotes the whole realm of manifested effects.

25.word_for_word: asya ca upalakṣaṇatvena viṣayatvam — this cosmic body serves as the indicated support for meditation; vastutaḥ tu — but in reality; virāḍ-jīva-niyantā bhagavān eva viṣayaḥ — Bhagavān, the controller of the living principle within Virāṭ, is the true object; aṇḍa-kośa-antar-vartini kaṭāhaḥ eva pṛthivī-āvaraṇam — the shell within the cosmic egg is itself the earth-covering; tataḥ ap-tejo-vāyu-ākāśa-ahaṅkāra-mahat-tattvāni — then water, fire, air, ether, ahaṅkāra and mahat; iti sapta — thus seven coverings.
25.translation: The cosmic body is used as an indicated support for meditation, but in reality the true object is Bhagavān Himself, the controller of the living principle within Virāṭ. The shell within the cosmic egg is counted as the covering of earth; beyond it are water, fire, air, ether, ahaṅkāra and mahat, making seven coverings in all.

26.word_for_word: virāḍ-deha-tad-jīva-tad-antaryāmiṇām abhedam āropya upāsanam kartavyam — meditation is to be performed by superimposing non-difference among the Virāṭ body, its living principle, and its indwelling Lord; pātālam pāda-mūlam — Pātāla is the sole/base of the foot; pādasya adho-bhāgam — the lower part of the foot; pātāla-ādīnām tad-avayavatā vidhīyate — Pātāla and the other worlds are assigned as His limbs; pātāla-ādīni atala-antāni — from Pātāla through Atala; adhastanāt ārabhya sapta bhū-vivarāṇi — the seven subterranean regions beginning from below; paṭhanti gṛṇanti — 'they recite/declare' indicates scriptural authority; pārṣṇi-prapade — heel and forepart of the foot; pādasya paścāt-puro-bhāgau — the back and front portions of the foot.
26.translation: Meditation is to be performed by contemplatively superimposing non-difference among the Virāṭ body, its living principle, and the indwelling Lord. Pātāla is assigned to the underside or base of His foot, and the seven subterranean regions from Pātāla through Atala are contemplated as His lower limbs. The word 'they declare' signals scriptural authority for this mapping. The heel and forepart are respectively the back and front portions of the foot.

27.word_for_word: ūru-dvayasya adho-bhāge vitalam — Vitala is in the lower portion of the two thighs; uttara-bhāge atalam — Atala is in the upper portion; iti jñeyam — this is to be understood; nābhiḥ eva saraḥ — the navel itself is the lake/expanse.
27.translation: Vitala is to be understood as occupying the lower part of the two thighs and Atala the upper part. The navel itself is the great expanse or lake corresponding to the atmospheric region.

28.word_for_word: jyotir-anīkam — the host of lights; jyotiṣām samūham — the aggregate of luminaries; svargam — heaven; mahar-lokam grīvā iti — Maharloka is the neck; gṛṇanti — they declare; tapo-lokam rarāṭim — Tapoloka is the forehead; satyam — Satya; satya-lokam — Satyaloka.
28.translation: 'The host of lights' means the aggregate of luminaries, the heavenly realm. Maharloka is declared to be His neck, Tapoloka His forehead, and 'Satya' means Satyaloka.

29.word_for_word: usrāḥ devāḥ — the 'rays' are the gods; tejo-maya-śarīratvāt — because their bodies are made of light; te bāhavaḥ — they are His arms; diśaḥ — the directions; śrotra-adhiṣṭhātryaḥ devatāḥ — deities presiding over hearing; karṇau — the ears; śrotrasya adhiṣṭhānam — the physical seat of hearing; śabdaḥ tu śrotra-viṣayaḥ — sound is the object of hearing; sa tasya śrotrendriyam — it represents His auditory faculty; evam nāsikā-ādiṣu api — similarly for the nose and other organs; nāsatya-dasrau — the Aśvins; nāse — the two nostrils; iddhaḥ — kindled, shining.
29.translation: The luminous beings called *usrāḥ*, the gods, are His arms because their bodies are made of light. The directional deities who preside over hearing are His two ears, the physical seat of the auditory faculty, while sound is its object and represents the faculty itself; the same pattern is applied to the nose and the other organs. Nāsatya and Dasra, the two Aśvins, are His nostrils, and *iddha* means kindled or shining.

30.word_for_word: dyauḥ — the sky/atmosphere; antarikṣam — mid-space; akṣiṇī — the two eyes; netra-golake — the eyeballs; cakṣuḥ — the visual faculty; indriyam — sense organ; pataṅgaḥ — the sun; ahanī — the pair night and day; rātri-ahanī — night and day; parameṣṭhi-dhiṣṇyam — the abode of Brahmā; brahma-padam — Brahmā's station; tāluḥ — palate; adhiṣṭhānam — physical seat; jihvā — tongue; indriyam — the faculty of taste.
30.translation: *Dyauḥ* means the atmospheric region. The eyes are the two eyeballs; *cakṣus* is the faculty of sight, and the sun is associated with it. The dual *ahanī* denotes night and day. *Parameṣṭhi-dhiṣṇya* is Brahmā's station. The palate is the physical seat and the tongue the sensory faculty.

31.word_for_word: chandāṃsi — the Vedic metres/Vedas; vedāḥ — the Vedas; śiraḥ — the head; brahma-randhram — the aperture of Brahman; sneha-kalāḥ — fractions of affection; putra-ādi-sneha-leśāḥ — traces of affection toward sons and the like; dvijāni — the twice-born things; dantāḥ — the teeth; ṣaṇḍhatvam ārṣam — the neuter usage is archaic; durantaḥ — endless; apāraḥ — boundless; sargaḥ iti yat — what is called creation; sa tasya kaṭākṣaḥ — that is His sidelong glance.
31.translation: The *chandas* are the Vedas; 'head' refers to the brahma-randhra. The 'fractions of affection' are the small affections directed toward sons and the like. *Dvijāni*, 'twice-born,' refers to the teeth; its neuter form is an archaic usage. The endless, boundless process called creation is His sidelong glance.

32.word_for_word: adharma-mārgaḥ — the path of adharma; asya pṛṣṭha-bhāgaḥ — is His back; kaḥ — Ka; prajāpatiḥ — Prajāpati; mitrau — the two Mitras; mitrā-varuṇau — Mitra and Varuṇa.
32.translation: The path of adharma is His back. *Ka* means Prajāpati, and the dual *mitrau* refers to Mitra and Varuṇa.

33.word_for_word: anantam vīryam yasya saḥ — He whose power is unlimited; vayaḥ — time; kālaḥ — time; tasya gamanam — His movement; guṇa-pravāhaḥ — the stream of the guṇas; prāṇinām saṃsāraḥ — the saṃsāra of living beings; karma — action; tasya krīḍā — is His play.
33.translation: He is one whose power is unlimited. *Vayaḥ* means Time, which is His movement. The stream of the guṇas is the saṃsāra of living beings, and their karma is His play.

34.word_for_word: bhūmnaḥ vibhoḥ — of the vast, all-pervading Lord; avyaktam — the unmanifest; pradhānam — primordial nature; hṛdayam āhuḥ — they call His heart; sa prasiddhaḥ candramāḥ — the well-known moon; tadīyam manaḥ — is His mind; sarveṣām vikārāṇām — of all transformations; kāma-ādīnām — beginning with desire; kośa iva — like a repository; āśraya-bhūtam — serving as their support.
34.translation: Of the vast, all-pervading Lord, the unmanifest *pradhāna* is called His heart. The well-known moon is His mind, serving like a repository and support for all transformations beginning with desire.

35.word_for_word: vijñāna-śaktim — cognitive potency; jñāna-rūpām bhagavat-śaktim — Bhagavān's potency whose nature is knowledge; cittam — consciousness/mind-stuff; mahim — the word mahim; mahat-tattvam — the mahat principle; antaḥ-karaṇam — the inner organ; ahaṅkāram — ego-principle; giritram — Girītra; śrī-rudram — Śrī Rudra; gardabhāt — from a donkey; vaḍavāyām — in a mare; utpannā aśvatarī — a mule is born.
35.translation: *Vijñāna-śakti* is consciousness, Bhagavān's potency whose nature is knowledge. *Mahim* denotes the mahat-tattva; the 'inner organ' here is ahaṅkāra; and Girītra is Śrī Rudra. An *aśvatarī*, a mule, is the offspring produced from a donkey and a mare.

36.word_for_word: vayāṃsi — birds; pakṣiṇaḥ — winged creatures; tasya vyākaraṇam — His differentiation or articulation; nāma-rūpe vyākaravāṇi — 'I shall differentiate name and form'; śruti-uktam — spoken in Śruti; śilpa-naipuṇyam — artistic skill; manuḥ svāyambhuvaḥ — Manu is Svāyambhuva Manu; manīṣā buddhiḥ — manīṣā means intelligence; manujaḥ puruṣaḥ — manuja means the human person; nivāsa āśrayaḥ — dwelling means support or abode; gandharva-ādīnām dvandva-aikyam — the compound gathers Gandharvas and the following classes; ṣaḍja-ādi-svara-smṛtayaḥ — remembered tones beginning with Ṣaḍja; asura-anīkam vīryam yasya — one whose prowess is the asura host; iti pāṭhe — in the alternate reading; asura-samūha-śreṣṭhaḥ prahlādaḥ — Prahlāda, foremost of the asura host; smṛtiḥ tasya — is His remembrance.
36.translation: The birds exemplify His artistic skill in differentiating name and form, as expressed in the Śruti, 'I shall differentiate name and form.' Manu is Svāyambhuva Manu; *manīṣā* means intelligence; and *manuja* is the human person, His dwelling or support. The Gandharvas and the related celestial classes correspond to remembered musical tones beginning with Ṣaḍja. In an alternate reading, Prahlāda, foremost of the hosts of asuras, is identified with His remembrance.

37.word_for_word: brahmā vipraḥ — brahma means the brāhmaṇa; tasya ānanam mukham — he is His face; kṣatram kṣatriyaḥ — kṣatra means the kṣatriya; bhujau yasya — who are His arms; viṭ vaiśyaḥ — viṭ means the vaiśya; ūrū yasya — who are His thighs; aṅghri-śritaḥ kṛṣṇa-varṇaḥ śūdraḥ — the dark-hued śūdra rests at His feet; nānā-abhidhāḥ — bearing many names; abhījyā devāḥ — deities worshiped in sacrifice; vasu-rudra-ādibhiḥ gaṇaiḥ upapannaḥ — accompanied by groups such as the Vasus and Rudras; dravya-ātmakaḥ — consisting of sacrificial materials; haviḥ-sādhyaḥ — accomplished through oblations; vitāna-yogaḥ — sacrificial performance; tasya karma kāryam — is the action to be done for Him; āvaśyakaḥ abhipretaḥ — intended as obligatory.
37.translation: The brāhmaṇa is His face, the kṣatriya His arms, the vaiśya His thighs, and the dark-hued śūdra takes shelter at His feet. The worshipable deities invoked under many names, including groups such as the Vasus and Rudras, are included in Him. The sacrificial performance, constituted by its materials and accomplished through oblations, is therefore the action to be performed for Him and is here intended as obligatory.

38.word_for_word: iyān — this much, of this extent; etāvān — so extensive; sanniveśaḥ — arrangement; avayava-saṃsthānam — disposition of the limbs; asmin — in this form; sva-buddhyā — by one's own intelligence; manaḥ sandhāryate — the mind is held in concentration; mumukṣubhiḥ — by seekers of liberation; yataḥ — because; vyatiriktam — separate from it; kiñcit na asti — nothing exists.
38.translation: This is the full extent of the arrangement, the disposition of the limbs. Seekers of liberation hold the mind upon this form through their own discriminative intelligence because nothing whatever exists outside the all-inclusive object contemplated in this meditation.

39.word_for_word: tad evam — thus; citta-sthairya-artham — for steadiness of mind; virāḍ-deha-jīva-īśvarāṇām abhedena upāsanam uktam — meditation through contemplated non-difference among the Virāṭ body, its living principle and the Lord has been taught; deha-jīvau īśvare pravilāpya — dissolving the body and individual living principle into Īśvara; saḥ eva dhyeyaḥ — He alone is to be meditated upon; sa-dṛṣṭāntam nirdhārayati — he establishes this with an example; sarveṣām dhī-vṛttibhiḥ anubhūtam sarvam yena — by whom all that is experienced through every mode of cognition is known; saḥ ekaḥ eva sarva-antara ātmā — He alone is the one inner Self of all; tam eva satyam bhajeta — one should worship Him alone as Reality; anyatra upalakṣaṇe na sajjeta — one should not become attached to the merely representative supports; āsaṅgāt ātmanaḥ pātaḥ saṃsāraḥ bhavati — from attachment arises the self's fall into saṃsāra; svapne bahūn dehān prakalpya — in dream, projecting many bodies; jīvaḥ tat-tad-indriyaiḥ sarvam paśyati — the jīva sees through the senses belonging to each; tadvat — likewise; īśvarasya tu vidyā-śaktitvāt na bandhaḥ — but Īśvara is not bound because He is the power of knowledge.
39.translation: Thus, for the sake of steadiness of mind, meditation was taught by contemplating non-difference among the Virāṭ body, the living principle within it and the Lord. The body and individual living principle are then dissolved conceptually into Īśvara, and He alone is established as the true object of meditation. He is the one inner Self by whom everything disclosed through every mode of cognition is experienced. One should therefore worship Him alone as Reality and not become attached to the merely representative supports, because such attachment produces the self's fall into saṃsāra. The example is dream: one jīva projects many bodies and experiences through their respective senses. In the same way Īśvara is the seer of all, yet He is not bound because His nature is the power of knowledge itself.
